why.correct: Sorted: 13, 14, 14, 15, 15, 16, 16, 31. With eight values the median is the average of the 4th and 5th values: (15 + 15) ÷ 2 = 15.0 drops. Forgetting to sort first gives the wrong middle pair.

Seven of the eight counts lie between 13 and 16. The single 31 adds a large amount to the sum, so the mean (16.75) sits above every value but one. The median (15) depends only on the middle of the sorted list, so the outlier barely moves it.
options: Correct. An extreme value drags the mean toward it; the median depends on position, not size, so it resists the pull.
The mean uses every value; the median uses only the middle one or two. That is exactly why the median ignores the outlier.
Repeated values do not stop you from averaging. A mean can always be calculated for quantitative data.
The range at 2% (18 drops) is the largest of the three concentrations, so these data are the least tightly clustered.

why.correct: Medians fall from 30.5 to 21.5 to 15 drops as soap rises. At 1%, both 21 and 22 appear twice. Ranges: 0% is 35 − 28 = 7; 1% is 24 − 19 = 5. The largest 1% count (24) is below the smallest 0% count (28), so the sets do not overlap. Removing the 31 leaves seven values, and the 4th of 13, 14, 14, 15, 15, 16, 16 is still 15.
options: Supported: mean and median both fall at each step up in soap.
Supported: 21 and 22 each appear twice and no value appears more often.
Not supported: with seven values left, the median is the 4th sorted value, which is still 15.
Not supported: the 1% range is 5 drops and the 0% range is 7 drops.
Not supported: the highest 1% count, 24, is lower than the lowest 0% count, 28.

why.correct: The sum falls by 31 − 13 = 18 drops, shared over 8 values: 18 ÷ 8 = 2.25 drops lower (16.75 to 14.5). Re-sorted, the corrected set is 13, 13, 14, 14, 15, 15, 16, 16, so the middle pair becomes 14 and 15 and the median falls from 15 to 14.5.
options: Correct: the mean falls 2.25 drops and the median 0.5 drops.
The mean change is right, but re-sort the corrected data: a new low value shifts the middle pair to 14 and 15.
The sum drops by 18, but that change is shared across 8 values, so the mean drops by 2.25, not 18.
The mean change is right; the median depends on position in the sorted list, so it moves by a different amount.

why.correct: Range = largest − smallest = 23.9 − 20.8 = 3.1 min.
The means are 11.1 min and 22.1 min, close to a 1 : 2 ratio. The 100 g range is 11.5 − 10.8 = 0.7 min; the 200 g range is 3.1 min, so the 200 g values are more spread out.
options: Correct: center doubles, and the range grows from 0.7 to 3.1 min.
The centers fit, but the ranges (0.7 versus 3.1 min) show different spreads.
Longer times mean slower cooling, and spread says nothing about which group cooled faster.
Separate cups are expected: each mass has its own sample of six, and their centers and spreads can be compared.

why.correct: Specific heat is a property per gram, so 200 g must give off twice the heat of 100 g to drop the same 40 °C. Water's high specific heat (from hydrogen bonds between molecules) means that heat is large, so cooling takes about twice as long when heat leaves the cup at a similar pace.
options: Correct: same per-gram heat, twice the grams, about twice the heat to lose.
The molecules are the same in both cups; bonds between water molecules are hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.
Specific heat is per gram and does not change with the amount of water.
Evaporation happens at any temperature; it is not limited to near boiling.

why.correct: Continuous quantitative data are measured on a scale that can take any value between two numbers: temperature, mass and time. Counted drops are quantitative but discrete. Color and yes/no are qualitative (categorical).
options: Continuous: temperature can be 21.3 °C, 21.35 °C and so on.
Quantitative but discrete: you count whole drops, never 21.5 drops.
Qualitative: color is a category, not a number.
Continuous: mass is measured on a scale.
Qualitative: a yes/no outcome is a category.
Continuous: time is measured on a scale.

why.correct: Mean × n = sum, so the five values add to 9.2 × 5 = 46.0 min. The four known values add to 9.0 + 9.4 + 8.8 + 9.6 = 36.8 min. The fifth is 46.0 − 36.8 = 9.2 min.

An outlier is first checked for a recording or procedure error. If it is a mistake, it is corrected or removed with a note; if not, it is real data, so it is kept and its effect is shown by giving a summary (the median) that resists it.
options: Correct: investigate, then keep and report honestly.
Deleting data because it is inconvenient hides real results; it is removed only with a documented reason.
Inventing a value is not data; it makes the sample look more consistent than it was.
The mode is often unhelpful with measured data, and choosing a summary to hide a value is not a fix.

why.correct: Changing 9 to 11 raises the sum by 2, so the mean rises. Sorted, the set is 4, 7, 7, 11, 12: the middle value is still 7 and the range is still 12 − 4 = 8.
options: Correct: the sum goes up, the 3rd value stays 7, and the smallest and largest stay 4 and 12.
The mean rises, but the largest value changes, so the range becomes 11.
The mean rises, but the smallest value changes, so the range shrinks to 6.
The mean rises, but the sorted set becomes 4, 7, 9, 9, 12, so the median moves to 9.

why.correct: Equal means say nothing about spread. P's range is 2 drops; Q's is 13 drops. Wider spread means any single measurement from Q could land far from the center.
options: Correct: same mean, very different ranges.
The means match, but the ranges (2 and 13) show the spreads differ.
Wider spread usually means less consistent technique, not more careful work.
Repeated identical counts are expected with careful technique; repetition is not evidence of error.

why.correct: The median is the middle value of the sorted data (the average of the two middle values when n is even).
options: Correct.
The mean is the sum divided by the number of values.
The mode is the most frequent value.
The midrange is the average of the largest and smallest values; it needs no middle position.

why.correct: Sort first (the middle of an unsorted list means nothing), number the sorted values, locate the middle pair at positions n/2 and n/2 + 1, then average them.
Slope = change in y ÷ change in x = (50.1 − 20.0) °C ÷ (5 − 0) min = 30.1 ÷ 5 = 6.02, which rounds to 6.0 °C/min.
This is interpolation. At 2 min the 100 g sample was 32.1 °C and at 3 min 37.9 °C; halfway between is (32.1 + 37.9) ÷ 2 = 35.0 °C.

Extrapolation assumes the pattern continues outside the measured range. Here it cannot: once water reaches its boiling point, added heat breaks hydrogen bonds to turn liquid into vapor, and the temperature levels off near 100 °C.
options: Correct: extrapolation beyond the data, and a physical limit at the boiling point.
Data only show the pattern over the measured range; nothing guarantees a line keeps going.
The 200 g line has its own slope; it does not describe the 100 g sample.
Picking one minute does not fix the problem of predicting far beyond the measured range.

why.correct: Specific heat is per gram. With equal heat input per minute, doubling the mass halves the temperature rise per minute: 6 °C/min becomes about 3 °C/min.
options: Correct: same heat in, twice the grams to warm.
Specific heat is a property of water per gram; it is the same in both beakers.
Water has the same hydrogen bonding per gram whatever the amount.
Slope depends on rise and run, not on the number of points.

why.correct: Increases per 2 minutes: 18, 16, 10, 5, 1 mg. The curve is steep at first and flattens as it approaches 50 mg.
options: Correct: the increments shrink and the curve plateaus.
The increments shrink from 18 mg to 1 mg; they are not equal.
This is the reverse of the pattern: the biggest increases come first.
The mass never falls: 49 mg at 8 min, 50 mg at 10 min.

why.correct: Slope = (34 − 0) mg ÷ (4 − 0) min = 8.5 mg/min.

The maximum possible product is set by the polymer available: 50 mg of polymer can release at most about 50 mg of monomers (a little more, because each hydrolysis adds the mass of a water molecule). As the polymer runs out, each interval releases less.
options: Correct: the curve approaches the total amount available.
Each enzyme molecule comes out of the reaction unchanged and can act again and again.
The polymer is dissolved in water, so water is in huge excess and does not run out.
Joining monomers removes water (dehydration synthesis); hydrolysis is the breaking reaction.

why.correct: It is the control group: everything matches except the enzyme. The small slow rise (2.5 mg in 10 min) is the baseline the enzyme curve is compared with.
options: Correct: a baseline for comparison.
Matching volume is part of good design, but the tube's main job is to show the result with no enzyme.
The water tube has no enzyme in it, so it cannot show the enzyme breaking down.
The tubes are separate; nothing passes from one to the other.

why.correct: The independent variable (enzyme type) is categorical: there is nothing "between" enzyme A and enzyme B. Separate bars compare categories.
options: Correct: categories become separate bars.
A line implies values between the points, which do not exist for categories.
A histogram shows how often values fall in ranges of one variable; it does not compare named groups.

why.correct: Time is the independent variable (x-axis), it is continuous (line graph), and each axis needs a label with units. Scales must be evenly spaced numbers, not just the recorded values.
options: Reversed: time is set by the student (independent, x-axis) and temperature is measured (dependent, y-axis).
Correct: a continuous independent variable suits a line graph.
Readings at different times are points along a continuous scale, not categories.
A scale must be even (for example every 30 s); marking only recorded values can make the spacing uneven.
Correct: a label and a unit on each axis.

why.correct: A correlation means two variables change together. It does not show which (if either) causes the other; another factor can drive both. Testing causation needs a controlled experiment in which one factor is changed and others are held constant.
options: Correct: correlation, possible third factor, test with an experiment.
Correlation does not establish causation.
The data do not prove either direction; the units of a variable say nothing about cause.
Observational data can show a relationship (a correlation); they just cannot by themselves show cause.

why.correct: Points rising left to right show a positive correlation; points close to the trend line show a strong one.
options: Correct.
A negative correlation would slope down from upper left to lower right.
A trend line summarizes the pattern; points cluster around it without touching it exactly.
A rising line means boiling time increases with mass, not that it is constant.

why.correct: Equal spacing must mean equal steps (for example every 10 °C). Here one gap is 5 °C and another 20 °C, so a steady warming would look bumpy and slopes cannot be compared.
options: Correct: an uneven scale distorts the curve.
Showing the recorded values does not make up for a scale whose steps are unequal.
An axis may start above zero if it is labeled clearly and the scale is even.
Temperature is the measured response here, so it belongs on the y-axis.

why.correct: A histogram shows how often values of one variable fall into each range (bin).
options: Correct.
A line graph shows change along a continuous independent variable.
A scatterplot pairs two measured variables for each individual.
A pie chart shows parts of a whole and does not show a distribution over ranges.

why.correct: Variables decide the axes and the graph type; axes and scales come before plotting; the key, title and trend line finish the graph.

In seconds, the 65 °C times spread most (s = 24.7 s). But 24.7 is about 6% of 410 s, 8.2 is about 5% of 152 s and 3.2 is about 5% of 62 s: relative to how long each takes, the eggs vary by a similar fraction.
options: Correct: compare the size of the spread with the size of the mean.
A bigger SD on a much longer time is expected; it does not by itself show sloppier handling.
The same n does not give the same spread; the SDs differ.

why.correct: Heat breaks the weak interactions (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions) that hold a protein's shape. Faster molecular motion breaks them sooner, so denaturation and the visible setting happen sooner.
options: Correct: denaturation speeds up with temperature.
Denaturation breaks weak interactions; it does not make new peptide bonds, and primary structure stays the same.
The tubes sit in water baths for minutes; evaporation is not what turns egg white opaque.
Denaturation leaves the amino acid sequence unchanged.

why.correct: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean. B's 1.75 g/100 g is almost seven times A's 0.26 g/100 g: B's boxes range from 7.9 to 12.1.
options: Correct: same center, much wider spread.
Standard deviation is about spread, not about how large the values are.
A small SD means the boxes are consistent, which is good, not imprecise.
Equal means with very different spreads describe different products.

why.correct: SE = s ÷ √n. Halving SE needs √n to double, so n must be four times as large: 4 × 6 = 24. Check: 1.75 ÷ √24 = 0.357.
options: Correct: SE falls with the square root of n.
Doubling n divides SE by √2 ≈ 1.41, giving about 0.51, not 0.36.
Fewer boxes would make the standard error larger, not smaller.
Six times the boxes gives 1.75 ÷ √36 ≈ 0.29, smaller than needed.

why.correct: Standard deviation describes how much boxes really differ; testing more boxes estimates it better but does not shrink it. Standard error describes how well the mean is pinned down; it falls as 1/√n, here by about √10 ≈ 3.2.
options: Correct: SD is a property of the cereal; SE is a property of the mean.
Box-to-box variation is real; more sampling does not make boxes more alike.
This swaps the two: SE depends on n, SD does not.
Extra boxes can include unusual values, but the estimates settle down rather than grow.

why.correct: About 68% fall within ±1 SD, about 95% within ±2 SD and about 99.7% within ±3 SD.
options: Correct.
About 68% fall within ±1 SD.
50% fall on each side of the mean.
About 99.7% fall within ±3 SD.

why.correct: Mean = 70 ÷ 5 = 14 g. Squared deviations: 9, 1, 0, 1, 9; sum = 20. Divide by n − 1 = 4: 5. s = √5 = 2.236, which rounds to 2.24 g.
Dividing the same sum by 5 instead of 4 gives 80% of the variance, so the square root is √0.8 ≈ 0.89 of the correct SD: about 11% too small.
options: Correct.
Dividing by a larger number gives a smaller answer.
With small samples the difference matters: √(4/5) ≈ 0.89.
Only the divisor changed from 4 to 5, so the variance shrinks to 4/5 of its value, not 1/5.

why.correct: Standard deviation grows with the typical distance from the mean. Y's values are up to 10 g away; X's at most 1 g.
options: Correct.
Same mean does not mean same spread.
Values equal to the mean add zero to the sum of squares, which lowers the SD.
Any sample of two or more values has a standard deviation.

why.correct: SE = s ÷ √n is always smaller than s for n > 1, but it does not describe the eggs. It describes uncertainty in the mean. To describe variability among eggs, report the SD.
options: Correct: SD for spread of individuals, SE for precision of the mean.
SE is smaller because of the division by √n, not because the eggs varied less.
For n > 1, √n > 1, so SE is smaller than SD.
They differ by a factor of √n and mean different things.

why.correct: Mean, squared deviations, sum ÷ (n − 1), square root (s), then SE = s ÷ √n.
New mean = 371 ÷ 6 = 61.8 s. The new value sits about 1 s from the mean, closer than most values, and n − 1 grows from 4 to 5, so s falls from about 3.16 to about 2.86 s.

The mean moves from 62 to 61.8 s, and a value close to the mean lowers the SD rather than raising it.
The new mean is 61.8 s, not 61 s, and the SD changes because n − 1 and the sum of squares both change.
Both statistics change a little; they use every value.

why.correct: Average rate = total change ÷ total time = (3.6 − 0) mm ÷ (10 − 0) min = 0.36 mm/min.
Interval rates: 0-2 min, 1.6 ÷ 2 = 0.8; 2-4 min, 0.35; 4-6 min, 0.25; 6-8 min, 0.2; 8-10 min, 0.2 mm/min. The curve gets less steep, so the rate falls.
options: Correct: the slope is steepest at the start.
An average over the whole run hides how the rate changed within it.
A large depth at 10 min shows the total distance moved, not the rate at that time.
The depth still rose from 3.2 to 3.6 mm between 8 and 10 minutes, so the rate was 0.2 mm/min, not zero.

why.correct: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient. Near the surface early on, high concentration outside sits right next to zero inside: a steep gradient. As the colored zone thickens, the same drop in concentration is spread over more distance, so net movement at the front slows.
options: Correct: a shallower gradient gives slower net diffusion.
Molecules do not change size as they diffuse.
The cube's size is fixed in this setup; the data describe depth, not swelling.
A large volume of solution holds far more dye than a small cube absorbs; the outside concentration stays about the same.

why.correct: Rates: 0-2 min, 1.6 ÷ 2 = 0.8 mm/min; 8-10 min, 0.2 mm/min. Percent change = (0.2 − 0.8) ÷ 0.8 × 100 = −75%.
The difference between two percentages is 97.8 − 56.1 = 41.7 percentage points. The percent change divides by the starting value: (56.1 − 97.8) ÷ 97.8 × 100 = −42.6%.
options: Correct: points for the difference, percent change relative to the start.
Percentage points and percent change differ unless the starting value is 100.
The difference between the two values is 41.7 points, not 42.6.
Percent change divides by the starting value (97.8), not the final one.

why.correct: Depth reached is the same, but the 3 cm cube has only 2.0 cm² of surface per cm³ of volume, against 6.0 for the 1 cm cube, so less of its interior lies within 3.6 mm of a face.
options: Correct: falling SA : V means a smaller fraction is supplied.
More total color may enter a big cube, but the claim about rate per cube ignores how much volume must be reached.
The depth was the same, 3.6 mm, in every cube.
Equal depth is the point: equal depth reaches a smaller share of a larger cube.

why.correct: Surface area grows with the side squared (×4) and volume with the side cubed (×8), so SA : V changes by 4 ÷ 8 = ½. The table shows it: 1 cm cube 6.0, 2 cm cube 3.0 cm⁻¹.
options: Correct: SA ×4, V ×8, ratio ×½.
Volume grows faster than surface area, so the ratio falls.
Same shape does not mean same ratio; the ratio depends on size.
Volume grows with the cube of the side; surface area with the square.

why.correct: 1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m and 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, so 1 µm = 10⁻³ mm. 2 µm = 2 × 10⁻³ mm = 0.002 mm.
options: Correct.
This converts micrometers to meters, not millimeters.
A bacterium is far smaller than a millimeter, not thousands of them.
This would be 20 µm; there are 1,000 µm in a millimeter, not 100.

why.correct: Volume = (10 µm)³ = 1,000 µm³. Since 1 mm = 1,000 µm, 1 mm³ = (1,000)³ = 10⁹ µm³. So 10³ µm³ = 10³ ÷ 10⁹ = 10⁻⁶ mm³. Converting first also works: 10 µm = 0.01 mm, and 0.01³ = 10⁻⁶ mm³.
options: Correct.
This converts the units as if they were lengths (÷ 1,000) rather than volumes (÷ 1,000³).
This is the side length in millimeters (0.01 mm), not the volume.
This is the volume in µm³ with the unit changed but not the number.

why.correct: Average rate = (80 − 52) °C ÷ 14 min = 28 ÷ 14 = 2.0 °C/min (a decrease in temperature).

Heat leaves through the surface but is stored in the volume. The smaller flask has a higher surface area : volume ratio, so its temperature falls faster, just as small animals lose body heat faster than large ones.
options: Correct: higher SA : V, faster temperature drop.
The big flask loses more heat in total, but it has much more heat to lose, so its temperature falls more slowly.
Specific heat is per gram; it does not make different amounts cool at the same rate.
A larger mass holds its heat longer, which slows cooling.

why.correct: 400 − 50% of 400 = 200. Then 200 + 50% of 200 = 300. Each percent change is calculated on the value at the start of that step.
options: Correct.
A 50% fall and a 50% rise do not cancel, because the second 50% is taken of a smaller number.
200 is the count after the fall, before the rise.
This adds 50% of 300 to 300; the rise is applied to 200.

why.correct: Steepest slope means highest rate (the start). The average rate is the slope of the chord from the first to the last point. Any interval's average rate is change ÷ time, never change × time.
options: True: the steepest part of the curve.
False: the start is steeper than the average, so the rate there is higher than the average.
True: total change ÷ total time.
False: flattening means the slope, and so the rate, falls.
False: a rate divides the amount made by the time; multiplying gives units of mg × min, not mg per min.

why.correct: Intervals: 20 °C, 0.05-0.11; 40 °C, 0.06-0.14; 60 °C, 0.40-0.52; 70 °C, 0.50-0.74. Bars that do not overlap (40 vs 60, 20 vs 70) point to real differences.
options: Overlap (0.06-0.11 is shared), so the data do not show a difference.
No overlap: 40 °C tops out at 0.14; 60 °C starts at 0.40.
Overlap: 60 °C reaches 0.52 and 70 °C starts at 0.50, so the data do not show a difference.
No overlap: 0.11 versus 0.50.

why.correct: The 60 °C interval (0.40-0.52) and the 70 °C interval (0.50-0.74) overlap, so the difference is not clearly larger than chance variation. Overlap means "not shown", not "shown to be equal".
options: Correct: overlap means fail to reject the null hypothesis for this pair.
A higher mean is not enough when the intervals overlap.
Overlap does not prove equality; it means the data cannot distinguish the means.
A wide bar affects comparisons with that group, not every comparison on the graph.

why.correct: Selective permeability depends on an intact bilayer and properly folded proteins. Heat loosens the hydrophobic core and unfolds proteins, so large water-soluble molecules leak out.
options: Correct: a damaged barrier loses selectivity.
Heating does not change the substance's polarity in this way; the change is in the membrane.
Aquaporins are selective for water; they do not pass large solutes even when the cell is warm.
The cell wall is porous and gives support; the membrane is the barrier to dissolved molecules.

why.correct: With the same n = 8, the width of a ±2SE bar depends on the standard deviation. Cubes heated to 70 °C were damaged to differing degrees, so their values spread more.
options: Correct.
Every group had n = 8, and more data make the bar narrower, not wider.
Bar width depends on spread and n, not on the size of the mean.
Bar width comes from the data's spread, not from the temperature itself.

why.correct: SE = 0.30 ÷ √9 = 0.10. Upper limit = 1.8 + 2 × 0.10 = 2.0 µm²/s (the interval is 1.6 to 2.0).

options: Correct: no overlap between 15 and 25 °C.
The 35 °C interval (2.4-3.6) overlaps the 25 °C interval, so this difference is not shown.
A rising trend in means is not enough; the 25-35 °C intervals overlap.
A small n widens the 35 °C interval, but it does not affect the 15-25 °C comparison.

why.correct: With n = 4, SE = 0.30. With n = 16 and a similar SD, SE = 0.60 ÷ 4 = 0.15, halving the interval; a real difference could then show as non-overlapping bars.
options: Correct: a larger n gives a narrower interval.
Switching what the bars show does not make a comparison of means more reliable.
Deleting inconvenient data is not a valid fix.
A 45 °C test answers a different question; it does not test 25 versus 35 °C.

why.correct: The 95% confidence interval is about x̄ ± 2SE, where SE = s ÷ √n.
options: Correct.
x̄ ± 2s describes where about 95% of individual values fall, not where the true mean lies.
± 1 SE gives a much narrower interval (about 68%).
The range is not used for confidence intervals.

why.correct: The overlap rule applies to 95% confidence interval bars. SE bars are half as long, so non-overlapping SE bars are weaker evidence. A graph must say what its error bars show.
options: Correct.
The rule depends on what the bars are; ±1 SE bars can fail to overlap even when the CIs overlap.
There is no such convention, and the conclusion does not follow.
Ignoring uncertainty throws away the information needed to judge the difference.

why.correct: Non-overlapping 95% CI bars indicate a difference unlikely to arise by chance, so the null hypothesis is rejected. That supports, but does not prove, an effect.
options: Correct.
Data support hypotheses; they never prove them.
Different cubes in each group is normal; the error bars account for chance differences between cubes.
Non-overlap leads to rejecting the null, and a null is never accepted.

why.correct: Overlap of 95% CIs means the data are not enough to show a difference at that level of confidence. Slight overlap is common even when a formal test would find a difference, which is why "no effect" overstates it.
options: Correct: "not shown" is not "shown not".
Confidence intervals never prove means are equal.
A narrower interval does not make a higher mean significant on its own.
The comparison is overlap between intervals, not the gap against one interval's width.

why.correct: CI half-width ≈ 2 × s ÷ √n, so a larger n shrinks it.
options: Correct.
A smaller n makes the interval wider.
± 2 SD is wider than ± 2 SE whenever n > 1.
Rounding changes how the number is written, not the uncertainty.

why.correct: Mean and SD, then SE, then the interval, then the overlap check, then the decision about the null.
The line crosses 0% between 0.2 M (+5%) and 0.4 M (−5%). Zero is halfway along that segment: 0.2 + 0.2 × (5 ÷ 10) = 0.30 mol/L.
Ψs = −iCRT = −(1)(0.30 mol/L)(0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K))(295 K) = −7.35, about −7.4 bars. Sucrose does not ionize, so i = 1; T = 22 + 273 = 295 K.
No net mass change means no net water movement, which happens when Ψ outside equals Ψ inside. So the cells' water potential is about −7.4 bars. Water still crosses both ways; the flows just balance.
options: Correct: equal water potentials, no net flow.
Cell water potential depends on all its solutes and its pressure potential, not only on sucrose.
Water keeps crossing in both directions at equal rates; the balance is dynamic.
Plasmolysis happens in solutions much more concentrated than this, where cells lose a lot of water.

why.correct: 0.8 M sucrose at 295 K has Ψ = −(1)(0.8)(0.0831)(295) ≈ −19.6 bars, far below the cells' ≈ −7.4 bars. Water moves from higher to lower Ψ, out of the cells.
options: Correct.
Sucrose moving in would add mass; the loss is water leaving.
If the solution's Ψ were higher, water would move in and the cores would gain mass.
Sucrose does not dissolve cell walls; the change is water.

why.correct: A larger core gains or loses more grams in the same solution. Dividing by the starting mass removes that effect.
options: Correct.
Percent change can be negative, and it is here.
Grams lost or gained differ between cores, partly because of their different sizes; that is the problem percent change solves.
Balances read mass in grams; the percentage is calculated from them.

why.correct: Ψs = −iCRT = −(2)(0.1)(0.0831)(298) = −4.95 bars. NaCl splits into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so i = 2.
Solute potential depends on the concentration of dissolved particles. Sucrose stays as one particle (i = 1); CaCl₂ gives three ions (i = 3).
options: Correct: particle count, captured by i.
Mass is not in −iCRT; sucrose molecules are actually heavier than CaCl₂ units.
Charge is not what i counts; i counts particles.
Ions attract water by hydrogen bonding and charge attraction, not covalent bonds.

why.correct: Equal molarity is not equal water potential. NaCl gives twice as many particles, so its Ψ is lower, and water moves from the bag (−2.48 bars) to the beaker (−4.95 bars).
options: Correct.
Particle number, not particle size, sets solute potential.
Same molarity, different i: the NaCl solution has twice as many particles.
The membrane in the question lets water through but not ions.

why.correct: Water potential depends on i × C. NaCl at 0.1 M gives iC = 0.2. Only 0.2 M sucrose matches (1 × 0.2).
options: Different: 1 × 0.1 = 0.1, half as many particles.
Different: 2 × 0.05 = 0.1.
Different: 3 × 0.2 = 0.6.
Different: 1 × 0.3 = 0.3.

why.correct: Water moves from higher Ψ (−6.0, the cell) to lower Ψ (−7.4, the solution). As water leaves, the cell pushes less on its wall, so ΨP falls (and Ψs becomes a little more negative) until the cell's Ψ matches −7.4 bars.
options: Correct.
